title: “WikiGameJam: Developing Wiki Games from Coast to Coast”
content:
The Wikimedia community has a long history of community-built games powered by Wikipedia and other Wikimedia projects. The Wiki Arcade website showcases many of these games, from WikiAsteroids (arcade space-shooter powered by Wikipedia’s recent changes) to Redactle (guess the article from hidden words) to Catfishing (guess the Wikipedia articles based on categories).

There’s a lot of untapped creative energy around wiki-based games, both from people already building playful experiments on top of Wikipedia, as teaching projects and from the broader game dev community.  To channel that, we launched WikiGameJam: an event and space for people to turn that playful spirit into new and exciting wiki games. The goal is to build on the ways people already engage with Wikipedia, as a trivia trove, a creative rabbit hole, or a challenge to race from one article to another.

We hosted the first-ever WikiGameJam on October 3–5, 2025, in Brooklyn, New York City. The weekend hackathon brought together developers, designers, and Wikipedia enthusiasts to collaborate and build new games powered by Wikipedia, Wikidata, and other Wikimedia projects.

title: Making space for Sylheti: From a decade-long Wikipedia journey to Wiki Loves Sylotology
content:
Sylheti Wikipedia began as a long-term effort to create a space for a language that had been largely absent from the digital knowledge ecosystem. More than a decade after the first proposal, the project has grown into something broader: a community movement connecting language preservation, education, local history and open knowledge.

On 25 February 2025, the Sylheti Wikipedia officially became available to the public. For many people, the launch of a new Wikipedia language edition might appear to be a technical milestone: a new website, a new language code, and a growing collection of articles. For the Sylheti community, however, the moment represented something much larger.

It marked the culmination of a journey that had begun more than a decade earlier, when Wikimedians started working towards creating a digital knowledge platform for the Sylheti language. The proposal for Sylheti Wikipedia had begun in 2014, and after years of community-driven work, the Wikimedia Foundation approved the project on 14 February 2025. The Wikipedia officially launched shortly afterwards, using the traditional Sylheti Nagri script.

title: Nurturing the Community: Reflections on Attending Code4Lib Japan 2026
content: I attended the Code4Lib Japan Conference 2026, held on September 6–7, 2026. Code4Lib, established in 2003, is a community centered on library-related programmers and systems engineers, primarily active in the United States. Participation from Japan began in 2010, leading to the formation of Code4Lib Japan by those early participants. In Japan, the community is open not only to technical experts but also to librarians in general. Conferences have been held annually since 2013; this year marked the 14th conference, which took place over two days at Kogakkan University in Ise City, Mie Prefecture.

title: Coverage of Wikimania 2026: From Paris to the World
content:
This July, the City of Light welcomed Wikimedians from all over the world. Some 1,250 attendees joined in person in Paris, while nearly 2000 joined Wikimania 2026 online. In total, more than 3200 of us came together to participate in conference sessions, discuss collaboration around “Freedom, Equity, Reliability”, and celebrate the joy of contributing.

Two-thirds (66%) of those who attended Wikimania Paris in person came from outside the host region of Northern and Western Europe. According to this crowdsourced map, an estimated 105 countries were represented. More than a quarter (26%) of in-person attendees were users with extended rights and more than a third (34%) were under the age of 35, making this Wikimania an important part of connecting multiple generations of high-impact contributors.

From taking selfies with Baby Globe, to experiencing the impressive lineup of Lightning Talks, attendees have not been shy about sharing their favorite Wikimania moments that helped them celebrate the joy of contributing. Please keep your posts coming! We have also received your suggestions for how to make Wikimania even better and are inspired to bring many of those ideas to life in 2027.

title: In Search of the Region – Organizing Wiki Village Ganggyeong
content:
It sounds like a joke, but the weakest area on the Korean Wikipedia is Korea itself. At one point, the community even debated whether to fill the gap by translating Korea-related articles from the English Wikipedia. The reasons are tangled, but it comes down to a loop: the articles are in poor shape, so nobody wants to touch them; and because nobody touches them, they stay in poor shape. The Korean Wikipedia we have today is what that loop, left to roll on, has produced.

I expect everyone reading this is nodding along — yes, this is a problem, and some of you might have a similar problem on your Wikipedia. But how many of you would raise a hand and volunteer to sort it out yourself? And there is simply far too much of it for one or two people to take on. What is needed, then, is something that pushes people into going out, finding sources for themselves, and building Korea-related articles up.

The Wiki Village Project was created to be that something. We took our starting point from Japan’s Wikipedia Town, but where those events are led by local residents, we chose a form in which editors travel to the town instead.

title: Wikicamp Kurdistan 2026: A New Space for Open Knowledge
content:
What happens when people who have never edited Wikipedia before sit down with experienced editors, learn the basics, and then go out and inform their community?

This was the idea behind Wikipedia Camp Kurdistan 2026, a three-day gathering in Erbil that brought together Wikimedia communities, new contributors, and young people interested in open knowledge.

Organized by Wikimedia Kurdish, Wikimedia Kuwait and Wikimedia Iraq, in partnership with the Erbil Youth hub Center as a local partner, the camp provided a space for participants to learn about Wikipedia and Wikimedia Commons and to meet the people behind the movement.

The first two days focused on practical learning. Participants learned about the Wikimedia movement, how to edit Wikipedia, contribute images to Wikimedia Commons, and participate in collaborative editing activities in two languages: Kurdish and Arabic.

The sessions were conducted in both Kurdish and Arabic, making Wikimedia projects more accessible to people from diverse linguistic backgrounds.

title: Let’s Connect, a peer-to-peer learning program: The shift to a community-organized model
content:
In 2025, Let’s Connect began its transition from a Foundation-organized program to a community-organized one. Today, anyone or any group in the movement can adopt or adapt the Let’s Connect peer-to-peer learning program to their local and regional context using the Toolkit and the resources and materials collected from the 70+ learning clinics organized over three years. The shift to a community-organized model began through pilot initiatives and discussions with ESEAP Hub, Wikimedia Iraq and Volunteer Supporters Network. You can read about the key learnings here. Our hope is that by using the toolkit, communities can leverage the tried and tested methodologies and templates of Let’s Connect to organize local, multilingual, and audience-relevant clinics. 

Why the Let’s Connect model?

Peer-to-peer learning is not unique to Let’s Connect, and many valuable learning spaces already exist across the Wikimedia movement. What Let’s Connect contributes, however, is a documented and adaptable methodology for intentionally creating these spaces, informed by experience running more than 70 learning clinics across different regions, languages, projects, and experience levels.

title: Setting our sights on Wikimanía Santiago
content:
As the sun sets over the Seine and Wikipedia’s 25th year draws to a close, we set our sights on Santiago. Sitting at the foot of the Andes mountains – the largest mountain range on land spanning seven South American countries – the city embodies the cultural richness, diversity and dynamism of the region. 

The Wikimedia movement also faces unprecedented change. The open spirit that once defined the Internet is at an inflection point, under threat from increasing concentration in the hands of few, surveillance, geopolitical fragmentation, and changes to the technological landscape. Against this backdrop, Santiago offers a powerful setting for the Wikimedia movement to come together and respond to a fundamental question: What kind of Internet do we want?

title: One day to celebrate and reflect with Wikimedia Community User Group Malaysia
content:
On 30 August 2026 in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, 27 community members were invited from across the country to attend the annual strategic meeting of Wikimedia Community User Group Malaysia. As a programme manager for ESEAP Hub, I was invited to attend and had the privilege to learn from local leaders gathering from Sabah, Sarawak, and West Malaysian communities. I shared the vision of ESEAP Hub as a service provider for East Asia, Southeast Asia, and the Pacific region. 

For ESEAP Hub, WCUGM’s role is instrumental in the establishment and implementation of Hub’s theory of change. Four Wikimedians from Malaysia take part as ESEAP Community Connector and drive the leadership as members of the Steering Committee. In the coming months, ESEAP Hub will collaborate with WCUGM in project partnership for training of trainers on AI, indigenous communities, and gender responsiveness within the ESEAP region. Our ongoing discussion to support Brunei Darussalam will also hopefully be realized by the end of the year.
